thread.title: After the Bell: The S&P 500 Is Having a Wonderful August but Should We Worry About September? - Barron's

author: Ben Levisohn
title: After the Bell: The S&P 500 Is Having a Wonderful August but Should We Worry About September? - Barron's
text:
By Ben Levisohn Updated Aug. 29, 2018 6:12 p.m. ET Illustration: Spencer Platt/Getty Images Higher and Higher . Yes, the Dow Jones Industrial Average crawled higher, and the S&P 500 closed at a new all-time high, but the Nasdaq Composite was the center of action thanks to a shift towards more growth-oriented sectors such as technology, consumer discretionary. Exhibit A: Amazon.com (AMZN) gained more than 3% and edged closer to joining Apple (AAPL) in the $1 trillion-valuation club . In today's After the Bell, we...
•...worry about stocks in September;
•...explain why Tiffany (TIF) tumbled to the bottom of the S&P 500;
•...highlight Marathon Oil 's (MRO) rise to the top of the benchmark.
It Doesn't Get Much Better Than This Can a freight train runaway uphill? Because that's what the market seems to be doing.
On a day with little market-moving news, stocks found a reason to head higher anyway. The S&P 500 rose 0.6% to 2914.04, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 60.55 points, or 0.2%, to 26,124.57. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1% to 8109.69. That left the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq at new highs, and the Dow just 1.9% away from its own.
Wall Street is now in the longest bull market in history. How did it get there? WSJ's Ken Brown walks us through the record-breaking bull run. Photo illustration: Heather Seidel/The Wall Street Journal In fact, it's been an August to remember. With just two more trading days left in the month, the S&P 500, up 3.5%, is on pace for its best August since 2014. If it gains another 0.3%, it would be the best August since 2000. Yes, that brings up bad memories, and there are still worries about a double top , even with the S&P 500 finally breaking its Jan. 26 high. But there's good reason for the market to rally, writes Brad McMillan , chief investment officer for Commonwealth Financial Network . Among his reasons: The Fed isn't worried about the economy , emerging markets aren't threatening to bring down the global markets, and the Trump administration's deal with Mexico shows that the threat of trade wars might actually lead to new deals, not just escalation. And all that's happened in a short period of time.
"[In] the past two weeks, three of the major worries that have been holding the market back have eased significantly," he explains. "With fewer worries holding the market back, continued appreciation in the face of strong fundamentals seems reasonable." McMillan sees the S&P 500 hitting 3,000 by the end of the year.
But that doesn't mean we shouldn't worry about September. NatAlliance Securities ' Andrew Brenner notes that it has been a historically bad month for the market. Bad. Really bad. The worst. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has averaged a 0.5% drop during September, and while that improves to a loss of 0.4% during a mid-term election year, it's still bad. "With the Nasdaq up 4.7% this month and S+P up over 3%, the last thing that investors want to hear is the history of equities in the month of September," Brenner writes. "No to those that think I am negative, just trying to keep reality in check."
Since when are paper gains real, anyway?
The Hot Stock: Marathon Oil Gains 5.2% Marathon Oil (MRO) surged to the top of the S&P 500 today as Barclays initiated coverage on the stock at Overweight and oil prices rose .
Shares of Marathon Oil gained 5.2% to $21.77, its highest close since July 10.
Barclays analyst Jeanine Wai acknowledges some issues at Marathon, but is bullish anyway. "Admittedly MRO screens mixed on our Fab Four Framework with strong free cash flow yield + growth and balance sheet, but weaker on NAV upside/downside & rate of change (core inventory depth) and capital efficiency metrics (recycle ratio)," Wai explains. "However, MRO’s solid execution, anchor Eagle Ford/Bakken assets, and Brent-linked crude oil exposure supports its best-in-class free cash flow yield."
Wai put a $25 price target on Marathon, up 15% from Wednesday's close.
The Biggest Loser: Tiffany Tumbles 4.3% Tiffany (TIF) sank to the bottom of the S&P 500 today a day after releasing earnings .
Shares of Tiffany dropped 4.3% to $125.48, continuing a slide that began after the stock opened up 5.9% on Tuesday but finished the day up just 1.3%.
Oppenheimer 's Brian Nagel , who cut Tiffany to Perform from Outperform on Aug. 10, sees risks despite Tiffany's solid earnings. "As we dig through Q2 results reported yesterday, we see clear indications of an ongoing, successful repositioning at Tiffany," he writes. "That said, certain factors keep us committed to our near-term more cautious posture for now‎. In TIF's updated FY18 outlook, management now highlights recent shifts in the U.S. dollar as a potential sales headwind."
Nagel sees risk of Tiffany falling to $120 in the near term despite having a $145 12- to 18-month target price on the stock.
